record.tranche_reason: The post reports a toy-model result showing incidental polysemanticity even when there are at least as many neurons as features. This refines the capacity-pressure account rather than reproducing the original superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The post reports a sweep-level experimental result for polysemantic neurons as hidden width varies. It also gives analytic collision arguments and a sparsification simulation with interference turned off, but the text does not state numerical outcomes for that simulation; those are not recorded as result rows. The article does not test the more-features-than-dimensions regime or LLMs.
record.test_reason: A toy autoencoder trained with at least as many neurons as features (n=256, m=256 to 4096) still develops polysemantic neurons at about n²/(4m). This is direct evidence that polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure (V3). It also qualifies capacity competition as the only account of polysemanticity (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that random initialization plus winner-take-all training dynamics can produce 'incidental' polysemanticity even when neurons are ample. They present this as a second, non-exclusive origin alongside capacity-driven superposition. They also suggest it could persist until m is roughly n².
record.recipe_differences: The post describes its autoencoder as similar to the ReLU-output model in Toy Models of Superposition, but adds l1 regularization on activations to induce winner-take-all sparsity and studies m≥n.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported polysemantic-neuron trend is examined across hidden widths m=256 to 4096. The post uses l1 regularization; it does not report a comparison of polysemanticity outcomes with different regularization settings.
record.problems: The post describes the work as preliminary. The empirical result is stated only as a trend over a width sweep, without separate numerical values, uncertainty estimates, or controls in the text. The setup uses basis-vector inputs that never co-occur, l1 activation regularization, and a simplified toy model; the authors also say their theory of the interaction among all three training forces is incomplete.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying experimental outcomes are stated numerically or explicitly in the text. The sparsification simulation is described as a comparison of theory and actual values, but its outcome is not stated in the supplied text.

untested.parts: The more-features-than-dimensions regime, near-orthogonal geometry and the sparsity-dependent transition are not tested (m≥n, basis-vector inputs).
Importance-based allocation (dedicated versus shared dimensions) when capacity is limited is not tested.
Only one toy setting: l1-regularised, weight-tied autoencoder with features that never co-occur. Prevalence in real networks and robustness to feature co-occurrence are not tested.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Per-width counts of polysemantic neurons from the 'Polysemantic neurons vs hidden neurons' graph. The graph is referenced but its values are not in the text. The linked notebook reports that all weights are near 0 or ±1.
missing.locator: Experiments section; author comment linking the TheoryOfPolysemanticity.ipynb notebook

record.verdict_notes: Preliminary Alignment Forum post. The empirical result is stated only qualitatively: the Θ(n²/m) trend holds and the 1/4 constant is 'fairly accurate'. No uncertainty is reported. A commenter (Rohin Shah) argues the result may depend heavily on features never co-occurring; this is untested. The l1 penalty is needed to create a privileged basis. The sparsification simulation reports no outcome in the text and is rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses m≥n, not more features than dimensions, and does not test the original superposition regime, its near-orthogonal geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
It does not test allocation by feature importance or compare dedicated versus shared dimensions under capacity pressure.
The evidence is limited to the post's toy autoencoder and its training setup; it does not establish how common incidental polysemanticity is in other networks.
No LLM activations or dictionary features are examined.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are tested.
The post does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.
